# Summarize Long Web Articles in Safari with Apple Intelligence

> **In short:** With Apple Intelligence turned on and a supported Apple device, Safari can summarize long articles from inside Reader mode. You'll need an internet connection for the first-time model download, and the feature isn't available in every language or region yet.

Long articles pile up — in your reading list, your email, your group chats. Safari, the web browser built into every iPhone, iPad and Mac, can now help you skim them with a built-in summary, using Apple Intelligence (Apple's AI system that runs on your device and in the cloud). This guide walks you through setting it up and using it, written for anyone who has never opened Apple Intelligence before. One honest note up front: the summary is a triage tool, not a substitute for careful reading when the topic really matters.

## Before you start
- **Device:** iPhone 15 Pro or newer, any iPad with an Apple silicon chip (M1, M2, M3 or M4), or any Mac with an Apple silicon chip. Apple Intelligence is free but only runs on these devices — older hardware simply won't show the option.
- **Software:** iOS 18.1 or later, iPadOS 18.1 or later, or macOS Sequoia 15.1 or later. Check by opening **Settings → General → Software Update**.
- **Apple ID and language:** signed in to your device, and your device language set to one Apple has rolled the feature out to — many features only appear in English at first.
- **Internet:** needed for the first-time AI model download.
- **Total time:** about 5 minutes the first time (mostly the model download), then under two minutes per article once it's set up.

## Step 1 — Turn on Apple Intelligence
Open the **Settings** app — the gray gears icon on your iPhone or iPad home screen, or in the Applications folder on Mac. Scroll down until you see a section labeled something like **Apple Intelligence & Siri**, then tap or click it. On the next screen, look for a toggle that reads something like **Turn On Apple Intelligence** or **Get Apple Intelligence**, and tap or click it.

Your device starts downloading the AI models in the background. A progress bar appears and the device may warm up slightly. The first download takes a few minutes, so leave it plugged in.

If you don't see any Apple Intelligence option at all, your device is likely not on the supported list, or Apple hasn't rolled the feature out to your region or device language yet. Some features only appear in English at first.

💬 Example: nothing to type here — tap the toggle, plug the device in, and wait for the download bar to finish.

You'll know it worked when the toggle reads something like **Apple Intelligence is Ready** and a small ✨ sparkles icon starts showing up inside apps like Mail, Messages and Safari.

## Step 2 — Open Safari and load a long article
Open **Safari** — the blue compass icon on iPhone and iPad, or in the Applications folder on Mac. Tap or click the address bar at the top, type a website address or tap a saved link, and navigate to any long article you'd like summarized. Pick something that's mostly text in clear paragraphs, like a magazine piece or a news explainer. Shop pages, dashboards, and sites that block text from being selected usually don't summarize well.

If Safari isn't on your home screen, swipe down on the home screen and search "Safari" from the search bar on iPhone, or check the Applications folder on Mac.

💬 Example: try a 2,000–3,000-word news feature on a topic you care about — a science explainer or a long magazine piece.

You'll know it worked when the page loads normally with the article text visible. There's nothing special to do at this stage — just open the article you want summarized.

## Step 3 — Switch to Reader mode
Tap the small **Aa** page-settings icon to the left of the address bar on iPhone and iPad (on Mac it's in a similar spot near the search field). A panel slides down with options that usually include **Show Reader** or **Reader**. Tap that option. The page reformats into a clean, distraction-free view — no ads, no menus, no sidebars — just the article text and images on a plain background. Reader mode strips the page down so the AI has cleaner text to work with.

If the Aa menu doesn't show a Reader option, the site may block it — paywalled news sites and login-required pages often do. Try a different article on a public site.

💬 Example: most major news publications offer a Reader option near the top of the panel — open the menu first and look there.

You'll know it worked when the page strips away ads and sidebars, leaving only the article text and images on a plain background.

## Step 4 — Find the Summarize control inside Reader view
With the article now in Reader mode, look for a way to ask Apple Intelligence to summarize it. In recent versions of iOS, iPadOS and macOS, Apple Intelligence adds a Summarize control inside Reader view itself — usually a button labeled **Summarize** or a small ✨ sparkles icon, often near the top of the article or in the Reader view toolbar. Apple has adjusted this placement across software updates, so where it shows up can vary by version and by device.

If you don't see Summarize right away, scroll slowly through the Reader view and check the top of the article, the bottom of the article, and any small toolbar or menu at the top of the Reader page. On some devices it appears as an inline option above the headline; on others it sits at the end of the article text. The Aa page-settings panel you used in Step 3 is for switching into Reader mode — the Summarize control lives in Reader view itself, not in that menu.

If you genuinely cannot find a Summarize option anywhere in Reader mode, the feature may not be in your software version yet, may not have rolled out to your language or region, or may not be supported on that particular article. Try a different article on a public news or magazine site before assuming the feature is missing.

💬 Example: nothing to type — slowly scan Reader view from top to bottom and tap Summarize (or the ✨ icon) once you spot it.

You'll know it worked when a short summary, usually two to four short paragraphs, appears either in place of the article text or just above it.

## Step 5 — Read the summary and decide what to do next
Read the short summary and decide whether the article deserves your full attention. If something catches your interest, scroll down to that section in the original — the full text usually stays available below the summary. The summary works best as a triage tool: a quick way to decide what to read carefully and what to skip. Treat it as a starting point, not the final word — on dense or unusual articles the summary may miss nuance.

If the summary feels incomplete or off-topic, the AI may be guessing. Open a second article on the same topic and compare, or skim the original before quoting or sharing it.

💬 Example: if the summary mentions a statistic or quote you don't fully understand, scroll to that part of the original article and read it in context before sharing.

You'll know it worked when you can tell in about 30 seconds whether the article deserves a full read, a skim or a skip — without reading every word first.

## Common mistakes
- **Looking for Summarize outside Reader mode.** Apple Intelligence's article summary in Safari only appears once you've switched to Reader mode. If you don't see Summarize, go back to the Aa page-settings menu, choose the Reader option first, and then look again inside Reader view itself — not in the Aa menu.
- **Assuming Summarize works on every page.** Paywalled sites, login walls, image-heavy galleries, and pages with very little readable text often won't show the option. Try a different article on a public news or magazine site if Summarize is missing.
- **Trusting the summary as a complete substitute for reading.** Apple Intelligence usually captures the main points well, but on very dense, technical or unusual articles it can miss nuance. Use the summary to decide what to read — not to replace careful reading when the topic really matters.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** When a long article pops up in your feed and you don't have 20 minutes for it, a summary tells you in 30 seconds whether it's worth the deeper read — a fast way to stay informed without falling behind.
- **For your business or work:** Researchers, students, and anyone doing background reading can triage a stack of articles in a fraction of the time — scan several summaries in the time it would take to read two articles in full.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one long article you've been meaning to read but haven't yet. Summarize it in Safari, decide if it's worth your full attention, and start building the habit from there.

## Try it now
Open Safari on your iPhone, iPad or Mac, load a long article you've been putting off, tap the **Aa** icon on the left of the address bar, choose **Show Reader**, then look around inside Reader view for any **Summarize** button or ✨ sparkles icon — often near the top of the article. In under two minutes, you'll know whether the article deserves your full attention — and you'll have a new habit for the next long read in your queue.
